description:
Video: https://youtu.be/q-m8K6G4aG8

“The bold jumping spiders, belonging to the Salticidae family, are named after their jumping capability. The exquisite coloration of the body makes them one of the beautiful spider species. They do not make webs for hunting, rather prefer to hunt by pouncing on their prey. It is the stereoscopic vision that helps them in stalking beforehand.”

They eat “boll weevils, pink bollworms, tarnished plant bugs, and tobacco budworms and smaller spiders” and are predated in by “lizards, birds, and dragonflies.” They live 1-2 years.

Source: https://spideridentifications.com/bold-jumping.html

“The jumping spiders, Family Salticidae, are bold daytime hunters with acute vision. They are robust and hairy, and they have a distinctive eye arrangement. The front row of 4 eyes has a greatly enlarged median pair. The second and third rows are moved back on the cepahalothorax. The spiders leap onto their prey and overpower it.

“The bold jumping spider, Phidippus audax, is a common predator of many crop pests, including boll weevils, spotted cucumber beetles, bollworms, cotton leaf worm, fall webworm, cotton fleahopper, lygus bugs, stink bugs, three-cornered alfalfa hoppers, leafhoppers, sorghum midges, mosquitoes.

“This species is variable in size and color. Individuals average around 0.5 inch long, but some individuals in Texas and Mexico reach 0.8 inch. The spiders are mostly black, and typically the top of the abdomen has a rather large white to red central spot and a pair of smaller posterior spots. The chelicerae are metallic green. Juveniles often have orange abdominal spots that turn white at maturity.”

Source: https://arthropod.uark.edu/bold-jumping-spider/

description:
This little Phidippus sp maybe P. audux I suspect has been living in our bird box for maybe several years? The bird box was going to be removed some years back has I had put up a new box about 20’ away. I guess the original box was preferred…birds nested. I normally clean the material out after they finish nesting or at the end of the season. … I saw one of the jumping spiders so I had left it alone. I don’t monitor the boxes much when something is nesting and various things have used it other than birds. Since chickadees started to nest in the new box I thought things would work out until a bluebird kinda chased off the chickadees but never used the new box. There hasn’t been successful bird hatchlings since. Something seems to happen to the young in the old box. The newer box has a medal guard that’s about 2’ long and more or less rotates when touched to keep predators out. Wasp took up residence in this predator guard so when I saw the wasp were starting to nest in the old box I decided nope not this time and ran them out and cleaned the box. This is when I realized the jumping spider was still there. I have him in a holding tank and am undecided if I should return him to the area. The debris I removed did have what I’m pretty sure is the remains of a small bird:( 
The original box was very popular at that location but the sycamore tree I had planted as grown so it’s not out in the open anymore. I have had bats and flying squirrels use the box so I hate to take it down however I wouldn’t want to set the birds up for failure. If anyone has any suggestions I would appreciate them.
